idiom_name: enum state + switch decider + SQLite instance row + timer_create deadlines
implementation_notes: Nothing in C supplies any part of the pattern, so all three parts are written by hand: an enum for the states, a switch (or a table of function pointers) for the (state, event) decision, and a durable row per process instance in SQLite or another embedded store. The rule that matters is that the row update and the outbox insert happen inside one transaction - a bare UPDATE followed by a send is the classic source of duplicated steps. Deadlines come from timer_create/clock_gettime or, more portably, from a sweeper that selects rows whose due_at has passed; compensations are ordinary functions called in reverse completion order. Hand-writing this is justified when the flow is small and no runtime may be linked in; past a handful of states the transition table should become data so it can be reviewed and unit-tested separately from the switch.
pitfalls: Process state held only in memory, or written without flushing/committing, is lost at the first crash and the flow re-runs steps whose side effects already happened.
A single global state variable instead of a row per correlation id makes concurrent instances interfere as soon as two flows run at once.
A signal-based timer handler that touches the SQLite handle or the process table is undefined behaviour; signal handlers may only set a flag and wake the event loop.
timer_create needs -lrt on older glibc and carries a per-process signal or thread configuration that surprises anyone reusing the process for other timers.
